summary:
Still in the Dark in Denmark
In the weeks and months leading up to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Copenhagen, expectations ran high that the meeting would produce a concrete emissions‐reduction framework to replace that of the Kyoto Protocol. As the discussions progress, it becomes more apparent that a resolution may not be forthcoming. With the first of two weeks of the IPCC coming to an end, the consensus on climate change is now under siege and hopes for the current session have been scaled back to yielding just a political basis for future negotiations (mind your pockets, taxpayers).

children.title: Rest of World: 10,292
children.summary: President Obama hopes Copenhagen will produce a new framework that includes legally binding emissions‐reduction targets for developing countries, especially China and India. It was the lack of such binding targets for developing countries which prevented Congressional approval of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol.

children.title: Intensely Level Playing Field
children.summary: China has tried to change the metric for measuring progress on emissions reduction from total emissions to one of emissions intensity. The concept of carbon intensity measures emissions per unit of GDP and allows China to highlight that while it is the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter by volume, it has much lower per capita emissions than the United States and other industrialized countries.

children.title: GDP Per Capita
children.summary: The European Union has announced it will provide $150 billion to developing nations each year through 2020 and proposed a system under which poorer countries would be legally required to take specific actions as developed countries continue to work towards assigned national targets. Earlier this year, China suggested that developed nations commit one percent of their GDP to developing countries' efforts to limit their emissions.

children.title: Its Only Money
children.summary: When the Copenhagen conference began, industrialized countries responded by endorsing a proposal for a $10 billion per year fund to be transferred to developing countries to help them with the potential impact of climate change. In the opening days of the conference, the White House said a consensus was forming around the idea, which it said would form a core element of any agreement produced in Copenhagen.
